title: Polynomial associated graded structure after quotienting by an initial segment
statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring, let $b\geq0$, and let $f_1,\ldots,f_b\in A$. Put $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_b)$ and $C=A/J$ [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. Suppose that the canonical graded $C$-algebra homomorphism
$$C[T_1,\ldots,T_b]\longrightarrow\operatorname{gr}_J(A),\qquad T_j\longmapsto[f_j]_1,$$
is an isomorphism [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring, def-weil-pbc-associated-graded-ring]. For every integer $i$ with $0\leq i\leq b$, put $I_i=(f_1,\ldots,f_i)$ (with $I_0=0$), $B_i=A/I_i$, and $\overline J_i=(\overline f_{i+1},\ldots,\overline f_b)\subseteq B_i$, where $\overline f_j$ denotes the image of $f_j$ in $B_i$. Identify $B_i/\overline J_i$ with $C$ by the map induced by $a\mapsto a\bmod J$. Then the canonical graded $C$-algebra homomorphism
$$C[T_{i+1},\ldots,T_b]\longrightarrow\operatorname{gr}_{\overline J_i}(B_i),\qquad T_j\longmapsto[\overline f_j]_1,$$
is an isomorphism. Polynomial rings on no variables mean $C$.

source.place: Tag 061R, lemma-truncate-quasi-regular, specialized to M=A; Tag 061P, definition-quasi-regular-sequence, and Tag 061N, equation-quasi-regular, expand the quasi-regular hypothesis and conclusion.

proof.text: We first prove the one-generator quotient assertion for every commutative ring and every sequence of positive length $b$ satisfying the hypothesis. Put $t=f_1$, $B=A/(t)$, and let $q:A\to B$ be the quotient map. Put $K=(q(f_2),\ldots,q(f_b))$. Since $q(t)=0$, expanding products of generators gives $q(J^n)=K^n$ for all $n\geq0$, with $q(J^0)=B$. Also $B/K=C$: the map $a\bmod(t)\mapsto a\bmod J$ is surjective, and its kernel is $K$, because $J=(t,f_2,\ldots,f_b)$. These are statements about representatives and the quotient kernel in [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient].

source.place: Tag 061R, lemma-truncate-quasi-regular, opening reduction and definition of the quotient ideal.

proof.text: Write $G_n=J^n/J^{n+1}$ and $\Phi:C[T_1,\ldots,T_b]\xrightarrow{\sim}\bigoplus_nG_n$ for the assumed graded isomorphism. Multiplication by $T_1$ is injective: in the coefficient description of [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] it shifts an exponent $\alpha$ to $\alpha+e_1$, and these shifted exponents are distinct. Thus for any $y\in J^r\setminus J^{r+1}$, the polynomial $\Phi^{-1}([y]_r)$ is nonzero and so is $T_1\Phi^{-1}([y]_r)$. By the homogeneous multiplication formula (2) of [lem-weil-pbc-associated-graded-ring-structure], its image is $[t]_1[y]_r=[ty]_{r+1}$. In particular $ty\notin J^{r+2}$. This uses no cancellation by $t$ in $A$.

source.place: Tags 061R, lemma-truncate-quasi-regular, last sentence, and 061N, equation-quasi-regular, multiplication by the first variable.

proof.text:
For $n\geq1$ we claim $J^n\cap tA=tJ^{n-1}$. The right-hand side lies in the left-hand side since $t\in J$. Conversely write an element of the left-hand side as $ty$. For $n=1$, $y\in A=J^0$ already. For $n\geq2$, if $y
otin J^{n-1}$ choose the least $m\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}$ with $y
otin J^m$. Then $y\in J^{m-1}\setminus J^m$, so Step 2 gives $ty
otin J^{m+1}$. But $n\geq m+1$ and $ty\in J^n\subseteq J^{m+1}$, a contradiction. Hence $y\in J^{n-1}$. The descending inclusions of powers follow from the ideal-product definition: a product of $s+1$ elements of $J$ lies in the ideal $J^s$. Only a finite set of filtration levels was used; there is no separatedness or Noetherian assumption.

source.place: Tag 061R, lemma-truncate-quasi-regular, assertion $J^nM\cap f_1M=f_1J^{n-1}M$ and its initial-form argument, with $M=A$ and $n\geq1$.

proof.text: The maps $\rho_n:G_n\to K^n/K^{n+1}$ given by $[x]_n\mapsto[q(x)]_n$ are well defined and surjective by Step 1. They assemble to a graded $C$-algebra map $\rho:\operatorname{gr}_J(A)\to\operatorname{gr}_K(B)$: additivity, multiplication and scalar compatibility follow on representatives from $q(x+y)=q(x)+q(y)$, $q(xy)=q(x)q(y)$ and the formulas in [lem-weil-pbc-associated-graded-ring-structure](1)-(3). In degree zero $\rho_0$ is the identity of $C$ under $B/K=C$. For $n\geq1$, a class $[x]_n$ lies in $\ker\rho_n$ precisely when $q(x)\in K^{n+1}=q(J^{n+1})$. Choosing $z\in J^{n+1}$ with $q(z)=q(x)$ gives $x-z\in tA\cap J^n$, and conversely any such difference gives a kernel class. Thus the kernel consists exactly of the classes in $G_n$ represented by $J^{n+1}+(tA\cap J^n)$.

source.place: Tag 061R, lemma-truncate-quasi-regular, the displayed computation of the graded pieces of the quotient; representative calculation in place of an uncited quotient-isomorphism theorem.

proof.text: By Step 3, for $n\geq1$ the kernel classes in Step 4 are exactly $[ty]_n$ with $y\in J^{n-1}$. By [lem-weil-pbc-associated-graded-ring-structure](2), these are $[t]_1[y]_{n-1}$. Hence $\ker\rho_n=[t]_1G_{n-1}$ for $n\geq1$, while $\ker\rho_0=0$. Under $\Phi$ this means: a homogeneous polynomial $H$ of degree $n\geq1$ maps to zero under $\rho\Phi$ if and only if $H=T_1Q$ for a homogeneous polynomial $Q$ of degree $n-1$. Indeed choose $[y]_{n-1}$ in the preceding description and take $Q=\Phi^{-1}([y]_{n-1})$; injectivity of $\Phi$ gives the equality. The reverse implication holds because $\rho([t]_1)=0$.

source.place: Tag 061R, lemma-truncate-quasi-regular, identification of the associated graded quotient with the polynomial module modulo $X_1$.

proof.text: Restrict $\rho\Phi$ to polynomials in $T_2,\ldots,T_b$. In degree zero it is the identity on $C$. In degree $n\geq1$ it is surjective: lift a target class through $\rho_n$, then through the degree-$n$ part of $\Phi$, to a homogeneous polynomial $H$. Separate its finite monomial sum as $H=P+T_1Q$, where $P$ contains exactly the monomials with first exponent zero and $Q$ is obtained from the remaining monomials by lowering that exponent by one. Then $\rho\Phi(H)=\rho\Phi(P)$. It is injective: if $P$ in the remaining variables maps to zero, Step 5 gives $P=T_1Q$; the left side has first exponent zero on every monomial, while the right side has positive first exponent, so comparison of coefficients forces $P=0$. This argument works over any $C$, including the zero ring, by [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring].

source.place: Tag 061R, lemma-truncate-quasi-regular, conclusion after quotienting by $X_1$; coefficientwise surjectivity and injectivity written out.

proof.text: The inclusion $C[T_2,\ldots,T_b]\to C[T_1,\ldots,T_b]$ sends each remaining variable to the variable with the same name; it exists by the polynomial universal property and is the monomial inclusion of Step 6. Its composite with $\rho\Phi$ sends $T_j$ to $[q(f_j)]_1$ and fixes $C$, so it is precisely the canonical map in the desired one-generator conclusion, by that universal property's uniqueness. It preserves degrees. Every polynomial and every element of an associated graded ring has finitely many homogeneous components; the degreewise bijections of Step 6 therefore give bijectivity of the whole map (lift or compare each of those finitely many components). A bijective algebra homomorphism has an algebra-homomorphic inverse: for $u=F(x)$ and $v=F(y)$ its inverse sends $u+v$, $uv$ and a scalar respectively to $x+y$, $xy$ and that scalar. This proves the one-generator graded algebra isomorphism.

source.place: Tags 061R, lemma-truncate-quasi-regular, quotient by the first variable, and 061N, equation-quasi-regular, the canonical map; finite-degree assembly made explicit.

proof.text: Now induct on $i$ from $0$ to $b$. At $i=0$, $B_0=A$ and the assertion is the given isomorphism. Suppose it holds at $i<b$. Apply the one-generator assertion just proved, over $B_i$, to the sequence $\overline f_{i+1},\ldots,\overline f_b$ and its canonical isomorphism supplied by the induction hypothesis. Its next quotient is $B_i/(\overline f_{i+1})\cong B_{i+1}$: the map sending the iterated class of $a$ to $a\bmod I_{i+1}$ is well defined and surjective, and its kernel before the second quotient is exactly the principal ideal $(\overline f_{i+1})$, since $I_{i+1}=I_i+(f_{i+1})$. It identifies each remaining generator with the image of $f_j$ in $B_{i+1}$, and both coefficient maps send $a$ to $a\bmod J$ in $C$. Write $u$ for this quotient-ring isomorphism. It maps the remaining ideal onto $\overline J_{i+1}$, hence maps each power onto the corresponding power, by expanding products. Thus $[x]_n\mapsto[u(x)]_n$ is a bijection of the successive-power quotients, with inverse induced by $u^{-1}$; the representative formulas for addition, multiplication and scalars show that their direct sum is a graded $C$-algebra isomorphism. On each remaining variable the composite sends $T_j$ to $[\overline f_j]_1$, so polynomial uniqueness identifies it with the canonical map for $i+1$. This completes the induction, including $i=b$: then the remaining ideal is zero, its positive powers and positive graded pieces vanish, and its degree-zero ring is $B_b=C$. If $b=0$ the base case alone gives the result. Polynomial rings on no variables are $C$ by their monomial description.
